q: Does the RC+ZNE synergy survive when the residual 2-qubit noise is non-Pauli (e.g. amplitude damping / T1-like, or leakage into non-computational levels)?
basis: The paper's RC argument relies on Pauli twirling converting coherent noise into stochastic PAULI noise, at which point ZNE's linearity-in-noise-scale assumption becomes well-founded. Amplitude damping twirls to a non-Pauli stochastic channel, and leakage is not twirled at all by a computational-basis Pauli group. Our replication only tested coherent over-rotation + a small depolarizing residual, so this regime is untouched by both the paper and this reproduction.
next_steps: Extend the executor to add a Kraus amplitude-damping channel (gamma in {0.001, 0.005, 0.01}) per CX in addition to the coherent over-rotation, and separately a two-level leakage channel modeled as a 3-level qutrit with a small (10^-3) escape probability. Re-run the four-way sweep and check whether RC+ZNE still stays flat vs. epsilon or whether the extrapolation degrades. Free endpoints (local Qiskit-Aer density-matrix, argo:gpt-4.1 for judge) are sufficient.

q: Does adding virtual distillation (VD, M=2 copies) on top of RC+ZNE give a further multiplicative gain, or does it saturate at the ~1 mHa floor we observed?
basis: Our RC+ZNE result plateaus at ~1.1-1.2 mHa across all epsilon, apparently limited by the small depolarizing residual + finite N_rand=30. VD suppresses stochastic error at the cost of doubling qubit count and adding a Bell-basis measurement; if the residual is genuinely stochastic (as RC should have made it), VD should reduce it further by roughly the purity ratio. If it does not, the residual is not fully stochastic and RC-quality is the bottleneck.
next_steps: Implement a 2-copy VD executor wrapping the RC+ZNE call: run the same ansatz on 4 qubits (two independent copies of the 2-qubit H2 problem), estimate <H tensor I + I tensor H> / <SWAP>, and compare the resulting energy error at epsilon=0.10 to the current 1.23 mHa. If it drops by 3x or more, VD stacking is genuinely additive; if it stays ~1 mHa, the residual is RC-limited. All local, no paid endpoints.

q: Does the 9-35x reduction transfer to chemically-realistic small molecules that dominate NISQ catalysis / drug-discovery benchmarks (e.g. BeH2, H2O, or a Fe-S cluster minimal-basis fragment), or is the H2/STO-3G 2-qubit result a best case?
basis: H2/STO-3G at 2 qubits has extremely shallow entanglement structure; deeper problems (BeH2 at 6 qubits, H2O at 8, Fe-S at 12+) accumulate coherent error over many more CXs, and the RC-twirl-then-ZNE argument might either compound favorably (more gates = more twirl averaging) or unfavorably (extrapolation over larger noise scale factors becomes less linear). The paper claims LiH also works but LiH was not run here.
next_steps: Pick BeH2 in a 6-qubit parity-tapered mapping (coefficients available in Qiskit-Nature or PySCF-generated), build a UCC-SD ansatz, and re-run the four-way sweep at epsilon in {0.02, 0.05, 0.10}. Log CX count and total-gate depth; report the reduction ratio vs. CX count. Should still fit under 10 minutes on laptop CPU with Aer density-matrix if kept to <=8 qubits.

q: What is the concrete hardware-runtime overhead of RC+ZNE relative to a single noisy VQE evaluation on a real device (IBMQ, IonQ), and does the accuracy gain justify it in a wall-clock energy-per-mHa sense?
basis: Our simulation says N_rand=30 twirls x 3 ZNE scale factors = 90 circuit submissions per energy evaluation, vs. 1 for raw. On real hardware each submission has ~50-500 ms of overhead (compile + queue + calibration-look-up + result), independent of the shot count. A 90x runtime cost that buys 30x accuracy is a good deal only if the paper's coherent-noise regime dominates on the actual device that day; on shot-noise-limited or T1-limited devices RC+ZNE could be worse per-wall-clock than just taking 90x more shots of a raw circuit.
next_steps: On a free IBMQ open-plan device (e.g. ibm_kyiv 127q, available via qiskit-ibm-runtime free tier), submit the raw / RC / ZNE / RC+ZNE H2 circuits at fixed shot budget = 8192, log per-submission wall-time and returned energy error, and plot 'accuracy per wall-clock second'. Free credentials only; no paid endpoint. This closes the loop between simulator claim and real cost.

q: Is there an adaptive allocation between RC randomizations (N_rand) and ZNE scale factors that dominates the fixed 30x[1,2,3] recipe, or is the paper's static budget already near-optimal for coherent-dominated noise?
basis: The 30 randomizations x 3 scale factors = 90-circuit budget is a static choice inherited from the paper's Sec. 3.5. Intuitively, at very small epsilon the coherent piece is small and RC is over-invested (fewer randomizations would suffice); at large epsilon ZNE extrapolates farther and might benefit from a 4th or 5th scale factor. An adaptive scheme (e.g. estimate the variance across randomizations, allocate more N_rand only if that variance is large) could either match the accuracy at half the runtime, or improve accuracy at the same budget.
next_steps: Sweep the (N_rand, scale-factor-set) grid: N_rand in {5, 10, 20, 30, 60}, scale factors in {[1,2], [1,2,3], [1,2,3,5], [1,3,5]}, at epsilon in {0.02, 0.10}. For each grid point record energy error and circuit count. Fit a simple accuracy-vs-budget Pareto frontier and check whether the paper's (30, [1,2,3]) sits on it. If a smaller (10, [1,2,3]) is Pareto-equivalent at epsilon=0.02, publish as a savings note. All simulation, no paid endpoints.
